methodological_rigor.justification: This is a single-center retrospective cohort of only 66 patients with 15 cancer-specific deaths, with no reported power calculation and no external or internal validation of ROC-derived cutoffs for CD4+, CD8+, CD68+ and TICD densities. Using data-derived cutoffs then dichotomizing to compute Kaplan-Meier/log-rank and feeding the same binarized TICD into Cox regression is a well-known source of optimistic bias and inflated effect sizes, which plausibly explains the extreme multivariate HRs (TICD HR 30.8, 95% CI 6.39–148; lymphatic invasion HR 12.7, 95% CI 3.01–53.5) — the authors themselves acknowledge model instability. With roughly 15 events and multiple covariates considered in univariate screening prior to multivariable modeling, events-per-variable is far below the ≥10 heuristic, and no sensitivity analyses, bootstrap/shrinkage, or correction for optimism are reported. Hotspot field selection was manual and no inter-rater reliability or blinded scoring is described, and the SEMS-vs-TDT comparison invokes multiple tests without any multiplicity correction. Multiplex IF methodology (Opal panel, inForm algorithm with ≥90% accuracy threshold, triplicate fields) is appropriate but does not compensate for the fundamental analytic weaknesses.

clinical_relevance_loe.justification: Design is an individual retrospective cohort of consecutive OCRC patients at a single institution with CSS as endpoint, mapping to Oxford LoE 2b (arguably 4 given small size and non-prespecified cutoffs). The question — prognostic value of invasive-front TILs/TAMs specifically in obstructive CRC — is clinically relevant because OCRC is an under-studied, poor-prognosis subset for which risk stratification could inform adjuvant therapy decisions. CSS is patient-relevant, and the suggestion that SEMS vs TDT may differentially modulate the local immune microenvironment is translationally interesting but underpowered and hypothesis-generating. The findings are not practice-changing and would require prospective multicenter validation before informing guidelines; they score at the middle of the relevance range.

reporting_quality.justification: As an observational prognostic biomarker cohort, STROBE (with REMARK elements) is the applicable standard. Strengths include a clear patient-flow diagram (Figure 1) with explicit exclusions, defined inclusion/exclusion criteria, specified TNM edition, a dedicated statistical analysis section, and acknowledgment of key limitations (single center, small n, exploratory). Gaps relative to STROBE/REMARK: no protocol registration or pre-specification of cutoffs or primary endpoint, no handling of missing data described, no sample-size/power justification, no sensitivity analyses, no blinded assessment of IF scoring, and the biomarker-specific REMARK items (assay reproducibility across batches, cutoff rationale beyond ROC, patient treatment heterogeneity) are only partially addressed. No data-sharing or code-availability statement is present in the manuscript text; antibody details are relegated to Table S1 only.

novelty_literature.justification: The novelty is primarily population-based: this appears to be among the first multiplex-IF characterizations of CD4+/CD8+ TILs and CD68+ TAMs specifically in obstructive CRC, with a specific focus on invasive-front vs tumor-center spatial contrast and an exploratory SEMS-vs-TDT immunological comparison. However, the underlying biological finding — that high TIL/TAM density at the invasive front predicts favorable outcome in CRC — recapitulates the well-established Immunoscore paradigm (Pagès 2018, cited as ref 25) and multiple prior CD68+ TAM prognostic analyses (refs 15, 16), so conceptual and empirical novelty are incremental. The SEMS/TDT immune-contexture observation is a genuinely new angle but is underpowered and preliminary. Overall this is a meaningful but incremental extension of prior work into an under-studied subset.

writing_presentation.justification: The manuscript is clearly written and logically organized: the introduction motivates the OCRC-specific immunologic gap, the methods are structured by assay and analysis, and the discussion ties findings to prior CRC immune literature and to the SEMS/TDT management question. The abstract is quantitatively grounded (specific cell densities, p-values, HR) and self-contained. Figure captions are informative and standalone-interpretable with numerical values restated. Minor issues: the discussion is somewhat speculative about SEMS-mediated immune restoration given the small, non-significant trends, and the extreme multivariate HRs are not adequately interrogated in-text beyond a brief limitation note.

key_strengths: Addresses a genuinely under-studied subset (obstructive CRC) with a focused immunologic question
Multiplex immunofluorescence with Opal/inForm pipeline and ≥90% algorithm-accuracy validation threshold
Clear patient-flow diagram, explicit inclusion/exclusion, and well-structured STROBE-aligned reporting
Novel exploratory observation that SEMS vs TDT decompression correlates with invasive-front TIL density
Quantitatively grounded abstract and standalone-interpretable figure captions
key_concerns: Single-center retrospective design with only 66 patients and ~15 CSS events — severely underpowered for multivariable Cox modeling
ROC-derived data-driven cutoffs used both to define groups and feed Cox regression without validation or optimism correction, producing implausibly wide HRs (TICD HR 30.8, 95% CI 6.39–148)
No power calculation, no multiplicity correction across markers/sites, no sensitivity analyses, no handling of missing data described
Hotspot field selection manual with no blinded scoring or inter-rater reliability reported
Core biological message (high invasive-front TIL/TAM = better prognosis) is largely confirmatory of Immunoscore literature; incremental novelty
No data or code availability statement; antibody and cutoff details only partially reported
chief_reviewer.rationale: The study asks a clinically meaningful question in an under-examined CRC subset but is methodologically fragile: small n, data-driven cutoffs, and implausibly large HRs limit the credibility of the headline multivariable finding. It fits a tier-4 oncology outlet after minor revisions clarifying the exploratory framing and cutoff validation; tier-3 would require major revisions including internal validation and reanalysis with continuous markers.
